recipes.name: Scotch Bonnet Hot Sauce
ingredients_raw: 18 fresh Scotch Bonnet peppers, sliced and seeded

steps.text: Cook peppers, onion, garlic, oil, and salt in a large saucepan over medium-high heat, stirring frequently, 5 minutes.
Pour in water; cook and stir until peppers are soft, about 20 minutes. Cool to room temperature.
Transfer mixture to a blender and purée until smooth. Pour in vinegar and sugar; blend until mixed.
Transfer to a container. Cover and store in the refrigerator.

raw_recipe.headline: Scotch Bonnet Hot Sauce
raw_recipe.description: This Scotch bonnet hot sauce recipe uses Scotch bonnets, jalapeños, onion, garlic, vinegar, and sugar to make one of the spiciest homemade hot sauces.

review.reviewBody: I have been looking for a basic Scotch Bonnet / Habanero sauce for a long time and this is the best one I have found. I pretty much copied the recipe but omitted the Jalapeños and replaced them with more scotch bonnets. I also used jam sugar (that's what we call it in the UK anyway) which has added pectin in it and made the sauce a little thicker. Any ideas what the shelf life is in the refrigerator with this amount of vinegar? Thanks for posting it.

Fantastic method and recipe. I did adjust a few ingredients and measurements due to the volume of peppers I had on hand. I had 4 red scotch bonnets, 8 habaneros, 6 red Fresnos, and about 26 Thai chiles. I used a camper stove and cooked the peppers down outside in a stock pot, which proved to be an EXCELLENT choice. I increased the water and vinegar amounts by 50%, used 2 teaspoons of salt. After cooking and cooling, I blended with 1.5 ripe peaches and 1 teaspoon of sugar. Turned out incredibly fruity, garlicky and SO spicy. Flavor of habaneros really cuts through, and the heat from the Thai chiles is extraordinary. Because I used all red, orange and yellow peppers, color turned out BEAUTIFUL. Can’t wait to experiment with different ingredients using this method!

I made this but changed a few things.
I used 24 Orange Scotch Bonnets w/seeds (no jalepenos). 1tsp salt. 1/2 cup water. I can peaches. 2 small skinned Roma tomato's. No sugar.
I pureed it all raw, THEN cooked it. Much easier and faster than cooking it first then having to wait for it to cool. Plus, if you blend it afterwards, your going to have to heat it again to sterilize it before bottling. I used a small generic magic bullet knockoff and it worked perfect, didn't need to strain anything. It's not hot at all, you can literally dredge your taco's in it and it's all flavor, little heat. Trust me I don't like HOT stuff, this is great. I'll never buy bottled sauce again.
Oh and I grew the peppers myself. I think next time I'll use fresh peaches or pureed carrot.

This sauce is awesome. I have made this recipe a few times. Once with scotch bonnets, a couple times with ghost peppers, and recently with chocolate naga vipers (amazing). I omit the jalapenos as they turn the sauce brown. Best approach I've found is to start the onions, get them translucent, then add the garlic. Once the garlic is fragrant and starting to soften add the peppers. Cook the whole thing until the skins of the peppers are starting to get slightly blackened in a few spots. Then add the water. I fluctuate between covered and uncovered to try and reduce the water to exactly the desired volume for blending, while still cooking all the peppers. You do not want to boil off all of the water. Use a little less sugar for hotter peppers to keep the bite and a little more for sweeter ones. When using hotter peppers: COOK THIS OUTSIDE!!

Fire sauce! Yum. This recipe can be much easier with the help of a food processor. Throw in the peppers (seeds and all), onion, garlic, and a couple of whole tomatoes. Blend it all up and then put it in the oil pan, and the tomatoes give it enough juice so you don't have to add water. Then proceed with the recipe. Use any type of hot peppers. Make it doubled or tripled and freeze some.

This turned out really good. Very hot but very tasty.
If it weren't for all the slicing it would be awesome. I guess you could throw them in the food processor before cooking instead of slicing.

This was a great recipe! It was my first evet attempt at making a hit sauce, and I am pkeased with the results. I typically use Franks and have found it to be dull lately and I was looking for something with more kick! Well I have found it now. I used 14 Scotch Bonnet and 6 Jalapano. I kept the seeds from the Jalapano, but did remove the seeds from the Scotch Bonnet as this is big step up from a franks style sauce! While prepairing the peppers, I used the ziplock bags that you typically use for meat. While cooking, I did open all the windows in the kitchen area as I don't have an exaust fan above the stove. I didn't have an issue with the fumes while it was cooking. The end result was great, the peppers I bought were mixed colours (red, yellow and orange) so when those were mixed with the Jalapanos, it turned out to be a light green/yellow colour. For clean up, I cold rinsed everyting used for cooking before washing with hot water. Overall, it was easy to make, has a great taste!

I made this recipe, but I only followed the ingredients not the technique or preparation. Basically all you have to do is give to smooth consistency, and then cook it for 10 minutes. And cooking the sauce is optional. My way cuts down on your prep time and cooking time.

I strongly recommend this based plan recipe for hot sauce, whatever peppers you're into. Conservation is up to a year and that stuff is freezing friendly. You can add blend of herbs, spices, making it your very own sauce. Fourth batch since I tried it with Scotch, Ghost, Habaneros, Tree peppers. As far as I know, when Jalapenos are not available you can use mild peppers (in appropriate quantity to build uppon) and KEEP ALL the seeds of those beast. Dont waste precious capsaïcine! Red onions are the best and don't put that much sugar. Looking for Carolina reapers to update y'all :)

It’s so hard to find a hot sauce that really lives up to the name. This recipe is a total winner! I made it with only the scotch bonnets, but kept the seeds in and omitted the jalapeños. WOW!!! If you really like your sauce HOT, this variation kicks it up several notches and has that unique scotch bonnet flavor. A little bit goes a long way.. and it tastes amazing. I will never buy hot sauce from a grocery store again!
I replaced most of water with jalapeno juice and added a little relish.. also added a little lime juice.
Thank you! This is a great recipe! I added a teaspoon of smoked paprika and squeezed some lime juice in it. Great for all my Tex/Mex meals or even just tortilla chips.
Just an extremely hot sauce without any flavour of anything but vinegar salt and pepper ! I like to taste the ingredients in a chilli sauce ! You can’t even taste the onions or garlic for the heat

Made this for favors for my daughter’s wedding. I used all scotch bonnets and added lemon juice - left over from making her cake - but otherwise I followed the recipe. The fumes made me sneeze while it was cooking! It is undoubtedly hot sauce! Great recipe thank you for sharing. I will keep it and will definitely be using again.

Would rate it higher but the recipe should come with a warning. I’m in Canada and it’s November so therefore freezing. You should have your windows open and lots of ventilation as the fumes were like breathing in pepper spray and while I wore latex gloves to cut up the peppers my fingertips literally feel burnt.
Subbed bell pepper for jalapeños due to availability, yielded 18 ounces. Fruity and spicy with all the scotch bonnet seeds. Will be making again!

I made this recipe following precise ingredients and instructions. It was fairly easy to make. I used the sauce one or two times and the jar sat in the fridge. One member of my family dipped his fingers in the jars and his face puffed and became hot and red. Be careful, this sauce burns both your ends.
Great recipe. Smoke half the scotch bonnets (I used hickory) and it will be the best hot sauce you've ever had. Other good optional enhancements are lime/citrus and ginger (to taste).
I made this exactly per the published recipe and it is wonderful! I might try the habinero variant next, to match my wife's tolerance for heat
